The author described it briefly—“a beast of motion, never still, neither wholly animal nor wholly spirit”—before dismissing it as an apocryphal interpolation. Yet something about the phrase, the way it curled and uncurled in my thoughts like smoke from a long-cold ember, refused to let me move on.

I returned to the shelf the following day, this time armed with a magnifying glass and a notebook. Beneath layers of dust and neglect, the Dromomorph had left a trail of faint echoes. A manuscript from the 14th century, attributed to an anonymous monk, hinted that the creature was born from the frustration of the wind when it failed to reach its destination. Another reference, in a lesser-known commentary on Saint Augustine, suggested it was the shadow cast by time itself, trailing behind it in restless pursuit.

It was not long before I realized that the Dromomorph had never been recorded in a single place, nor had anyone who had claimed to see it ever agreed on its form. One witness, a sailor named Elias Thorncroft, wrote in a letter that it looked like a horse made entirely of fog. Another, a 17th-century naturalist, described it as “the ghost of a galloping hare.” And in yet another account, from a woman who claimed to have glimpsed it through a stained-glass window, it appeared to be a figure of pure velocity, its features erased by the speed at which it moved.

I became convinced that the Dromomorph was real—not in the sense of existing in the world as we know it, but in the way that certain ideas exist, persistent and elusive, like the idea of a name just on the tip of your tongue.

I began searching for others who had felt its pull. I wrote letters, visited libraries, followed trails of footnotes and half-remembered conversations. I discovered that no one had ever seen the Dromomorph and lived to describe it coherently. Those who had chased it longest had, in various accounts, either disappeared or gone mad. And yet the Dromomorph continued, slipping through the cracks of history, trailing whispers behind it like the echo of a hoofbeat on an empty road.

THURSDAY is for redundancies. At least, that’s what Mrs. Klinkworth insists, and given that she runs the Redundancy Bureau for the Tri-State Region, we tend to go along with her. Thursday mornings are when the machines hum louder, the clerks shuffle faster, and the teletypes start to twitch like agitated moths. It’s also the day the Redundant Word of the Week is announced.

This week’s word: **“Eventually.”**

Mrs. Klinkworth’s voice crackles through the loudspeakers in the Bureau’s vast, windowless hall, where a thousand filing cabinets groan under the weight of unnecessary phrases. “Eventually,” she declares, “is the linguistic equivalent of a stalled subway car full of commuters who’ve forgotten both their destinations and the time.” Her tone is neither mournful nor amused—just efficient, the way efficiency ought to sound when spoken by a woman with a monocle and a fondness for straight pins in the lapel.

The Bureau’s employees nod solemnly, many of them already drafting notices for the public. Eventually, they will receive them via postcard, stamped with the official seal of redundancy elimination, and printed in triplicate. Each letter will urge readers to reconsider their use of the word, offering polite suggestions such as *“in time”* or *“with persistence.”* Some will suggest removing the word entirely.

At Desk 7B, where the Redundancy Bureau’s youngest clerk, Elsie Trumbull, recently passed the third anniversary of her employment (a milestone marked with a single chocolate-covered espresso bean and a memo from headquarters), Elsie stares at her typewriter and wonders if *“eventually”* isn’t a beautiful word after all. It implies hope, it suggests perseverance. It is, in its own way, human.

But Mrs. Klinkworth would never allow that sentiment.

Across the room, a machine spits out a fresh list of words flagged for deletion. Next week: **“Interesting.”** The machine clicks and whirs, indifferent to poetry.

Elise leans forward, fingers poised above the keys, and begins typing the weekly announcement:

> TO THE PUBLIC:  
> This week, we draw your attention to the excessive usage of the word *“eventually.”* While it may seem harmless, “eventually” is often used as a placeholder for action, a crutch for indecision. In place of *“I’ll fix it eventually,”* consider *“I will fix it.”* Or better yet: *“I am fixing it.”*

She pauses, then adds, almost wistfully:

> Remember: *Eventually* is not a solution. It is a delay.

MARTHA HAD NOT intended to buy a parrot. She only went into the pet store because the sidewalk outside smelled of mildew and the sun, and she thought, Why not a little brightness?

Inside, the shop was a riot of color—plastic trees in fishbowls, neon collars, and birds who looked like they’d flown straight out of a child’s crayon box. Martha wandered past rows of cages until she saw the one at the back. It wasn’t much to look at—scruffy, dull plumage, one wing drooping slightly—but the bird had a presence. It cocked its head, blinked slowly, and said, “Hello.”

Martha blinked back.

“I think he’s trying to make friends,” said the shop owner, a woman named Gwen with a voice like a sigh. “He’s been here six months. No one ever comes back for him.”

“I’m not buying him to be a pet exactly,” Martha said. “Just… company.”

Gwen raised an eyebrow. “Company is what he needs. Or a lawyer.”

Martha took the cage home on the subway. The bird watched her, quiet. That night, when she opened the cage, he hopped onto her wrist like a tiny, trembling anchor. She laughed.

“I’m not your mother,” she said.

“Nor am I yours,” the bird replied.

By morning, she had named him Eli. He greeted each new day with a yawn and a question: “Is it time yet?”

“Time for what?” she’d ask.

“To be me.”

Martha stopped answering.

She kept Eli on the windowsill, near the plant that had died twice and still sat there like a monument. Eli began to talk to it. “You’re not dead,” he’d say. “You’re just resting.”

Martha left the apartment less. When she did, Eli waited alone, staring out the window. When the mailman came, Eli squawked, “I’ll kill you!” and Martha, halfway down the stairs, had to run back up to apologize.

Neighbors started to notice. One evening, Mrs. Ruiz from 3C knocked on her door and asked, “Is that bird yours?”

“Yes,” Martha said.

“He told me you were having an affair.”

Martha frowned.

“With the mailman,” said Mrs. Ruiz, helpfully.

Eli squawked in agreement.

Martha bought him more toys—a mirror, a chain of colored beads, a bell that jingled on a string. Eli learned to whistle “Clair de Lune” and once, when the power went out, he sang the national anthem in what sounded like Bulgarian. Martha began to suspect Eli knew things she did not.

Then one morning, he said, “They want to take you.”

“Who?” she asked.

“The people you don’t talk to.”

Martha laughed. “You’ve been watching too many horror movies.”

Eli didn’t laugh. He just stared at her, feathers bristling, as if waiting for her to remember something she’d long since forgotten.

And for the first time in weeks, Martha felt the chill of something shifting just beyond the edges of her life—something old, perhaps, but waking.

They had named it the Lurch, and it wasn’t a car. It wasn’t a truck either, though it tried. It had the soul of a dream deferred and the frame of something built on a bet, maybe by two drunk mechanics in a garage off Route 66 at midnight, somewhere between Amarillo and Albuquerque. The Lurch didn’t just move—it staggered. It lurched, as if unsure of whether it was meant to go forward, backward, sideways, or simply stop breathing entirely.

Its paint job, once a jaunty red, had peeled into patches like old skin, revealing underneath layers of rust, regret, and something that might have once been chrome. It hummed a tired hymn when it ran, which was often when it wasn’t running. Its engine coughed more than it roared, and its dashboard was a graveyard of blinking gauges and warning lights. The gas gauge, if asked nicely, would show the tank full. The temperature gauge, less forgiving, would always lie about heat. The speedometer, it was widely assumed, had gone to live in another state.

Still, the Lurch had its admirers. There was Marla, the mechanic’s niece, who claimed the car had a spirit. "She's stubborn," she'd say, running a hand down its side like it was a horse. "You don't beat the Lurch, you talk to her." There was also old Mr. Kline, who claimed he once saw the Lurch drive itself through a storm in 1973 and never stopped until it found a diner with pie that tasted like memory. “She’s got a heart,” he’d mutter, lighting a cigarette with trembling fingers. “If you listen real close.”

But the Lurch had one true master, and that was Dillinger—Dill, to the locals, though he rarely stuck around long enough for anyone to call him anything. Dill was a man of few words and fewer regrets, with a voice that cracked like dry earth in summer and eyes that held a history of places he hadn’t stayed. He drove the Lurch like it was a part of him, and maybe it was. He didn’t care about speed or status. He just wanted the thing to keep moving, because stopping meant questions, and Dill had no patience for answers.

One morning, just as the sun was deciding whether to rise or stay buried in the hills, Dill leaned against the hood of the Lurch and stared west. The horizon was bruised with smoke from the valley fires. The air smelled of gasoline, dust, and something else—something older, something like goodbye. The Lurch groaned beside him, waiting. Waiting for what, neither of them knew. But wait they would, because that was what broken things did best.

It began with a single typewriter, clattering in the middle of the library at midnight. No one had seen it arrive, nor had anyone heard the man who sat before it, fingers flying over keys worn smooth with decades of use. The librarians had long since gone home, and the building stood empty, save for the occasional flicker of a security light or the distant whine of a subway train. But this man—who no one remembered hiring—tapped away with the precision of a surgeon and the fury of a prophet.

He typed not for publication, nor for posterity, but for the sake of a correction. A single error, a single misstatement, had crept into the history books. A minor detail, perhaps, but one that, left unchallenged, threatened to unravel the entire fabric of recorded fact. He was not a historian, but a corrector of histories. And if no one else would do it, then he would.

The typewriter’s ribbon was dry and cracked, leaving letters smudged and incomplete. The machine coughed with every keystroke, its internal springs groaning as if in protest. Yet the man continued, undeterred. He wore a gray wool vest that smelled faintly of mothballs and lavender, and his eyes, though clouded with age, were sharp with purpose.

His correction concerned a minor figure from the Eighteenth Century—a certain Baron von Schrecklich, credited in most accounts with inventing the first mechanical piano. But according to the man’s notes, the credit belonged not to the baron, but to his housemaid, Eliza. She had constructed the device in the cellar, beneath the grand manor, while pretending to sweep floors and dust mirrors. She had done it in secrecy, fearing ridicule, and had left no trace of her labor except for a sketch hidden inside a hollowed-out candlestick.

The man had spent years tracking this truth, consulting obscure journals, forgotten diaries, and the brittle remains of correspondence that spoke in code. Only now, with the weight of time pressing in, did he feel ready to bring it forward. He typed rapidly, each letter a defiance against falsehood, each sentence a small act of justice.

And somewhere, in the vastness of the building, a clock ticked. A mouse rustled in the rafters. The wind shifted outside, rattling the windows like whispers from another time. The man did not look up. He would not stop until it was right.

THE FIRST TIME I REALIZED that parentheses might be dangerous was during a conversation at a dinner party, where someone casually inserted a thought into a sentence like this: “I went to the store (to buy milk, but I forgot) and came home.” The parentheses were harmless enough, but they left behind a ghost of uncertainty—a kind of afterimage of a decision not made, a path not taken, a thing forgotten. That night I dreamed of parentheses opening and closing in midair, each one containing a different version of the self—me at the store, yes, but also me buying something else entirely, me never going at all.

Since then, I’ve grown suspicious. Parentheses are not just punctuation marks. They are doorways, portals between statements, between choices, between lives. They suggest what could have been, but needn’t be said. And yet, in every sentence, they linger, like footnotes to a life already lived, to decisions already made. 

I began collecting sentences with parentheses, transcribing them into a notebook I keep under my bed. Some were simple: “He went to the meeting (though he stayed home instead).” Others were more elaborate, layered with parentheticals that nested inside one another like Russian dolls made of text. “She called (she didn’t, not really, just texted) and I said (what I actually said was no, but I meant maybe) that I’d meet her later (but I didn’t).”

The more I read, the more I noticed how often people used parentheses to rewrite themselves after the fact. To apologize. To clarify. To excuse. To revise. In this way, they became a kind of linguistic undo button, letting the speaker back out of something they’d already said.

But what if they were more than that?

Last week, I met a woman named Marla at a café. She wore a scarf wrapped in a way that looked deliberate and sad. When she spoke, she paused often, as if rehearsing what she meant before she said it. “I’ve always liked parentheses,” she said. “They give you room to reconsider.” I asked if she used them in her writing. She nodded. “All the time. They help me keep track of what I’m pretending.”

I wanted to ask what she meant by that, but before I could, she leaned forward and whispered, “You ever wonder if you’re living the real one?”

I blinked.

“The real one,” she repeated. “The one without the parentheses.”

And then she smiled—a slow, knowing smile—and slipped a scrap of paper into my book. It read: (This is not a parenthesis. It is a beginning.)

IT HAPPENED during a routine check of the [REDACTED] archives, deep in a folder labeled “Historical Anomalies” and buried beneath decades of misplaced memos. I was looking for something else—some directive on internal communication protocols from the mid-’90s—when my fingers brushed against a sheaf of yellowed pages stapled haphazardly to the inside of a dust-caked ledger. The title was smudged, but a few words still legible: *Project Echo*.

I don’t know why I opened it. Possibly curiosity. Possibly that strange compulsion people sometimes feel when they’re in the middle of doing something practical and suddenly stumble upon evidence that the world is not exactly as they believed it to be.

The first page was a memo, signed by a name I’d never seen but somehow recognized—the way you recognize the shape of a dream you’ve had before. The date was October 17, 1989. The subject line read: *Testing Resonance Between Past and Present*. The message was brief. It described a set of controlled experiments conducted in a soundproof chamber, involving a device known internally as “The Harmonic Tuner,” and a series of recorded voice samples from individuals who had since died.

What followed was a list—of names, dates, and brief summaries of events that matched precisely the lives and deaths of those listed. But the final column, marked simply “Response,” was where things became impossible to ignore.

One entry stood out. The name was familiar. Eleanor Whitman, born 1946, died 1987. The event was the collapse of a bridge during construction—a tragedy widely covered at the time. The voice recording, according to the memo, was made three days before the incident. The final word transcribed beside it was not “none” or “silence,” but “Yes.”

That’s when I started to read faster, heart beating in my ears, as if speed alone might make sense of the nonsense accumulating on the page.

Another entry: “James K. Riley, 1923–1988. Recorded June 13, 1987. Response: No.”  
Then: “No,” again.  
And again.  
And finally, on the last attempt, “Maybe.”

The implications folded around me like a slow leak of air in a sealed room. Someone, somewhere, had been asking questions—and someone, or something, had been answering.

I closed the ledger and sat still for a long moment, listening to the hum of fluorescent lights overhead and the distant shuffle of footsteps in the hallway.

It wasn’t until later that I realized I’d stopped breathing for almost a full minute.

Mildred Haskins had a theory about commas. Not the grammatical ones, though she respected those, but the pauses between people—the places where meaning, intent, and affection sometimes slipped through. She wasn’t a teacher, nor a scholar, but she was the town’s reigning expert on commas, and people came to her for advice when their sentences felt broken and their conversations fell flat.

She ran the only secondhand bookstore in town, "The Comma Stop," a name she’d chosen with deliberate irony, given how often customers would walk in with their words tangled and their thoughts in need of a pause. The store smelled of old paper and mildew, and the shelves sagged with the weight of decades of neglected wisdom.

On this particular morning, a letter arrived in a plain envelope. The return address was blurred, but the handwriting was careful, each stroke of ink precise and deliberate. Inside, it read simply:

*“Please come speak with me about the comma.”*

Below that, a time and location: the old train station, noon. Mildred hadn’t been to the station in years. It had been decommissioned during the war, repurposed into a storage facility for the town’s forgotten relics—railway ties, rusted signs, and a single bench that once waited for someone now long gone.

Curious, she folded the letter and tucked it into her coat pocket. She had always believed that the comma, more than any other punctuation, held the key to understanding the human condition. It was the breath between words, the hesitation between actions, the unspoken agreement that not everything needs to be said all at once.

At noon, she arrived at the station. The air smelled of coal dust and memory. The bench was empty, but a man sat nearby on a crate, his back to her. He was older, perhaps, or younger—age blurred in the way he held himself, like someone accustomed to waiting.

He turned when she approached, eyes sharp behind wire-rimmed glasses. “Thank you,” he said, voice steady but soft.

“You wanted to talk about commas?” she asked, not unkindly.

He nodded. “More specifically, the pauses they create. The silence they suggest. I’ve spent my life studying what is left unsaid.”

Mildred smiled. “Then you’ll understand that I’m late.”

He smiled back. “So am I.”

And in that moment, between the rusted tracks and the whisper of the wind, they began the conversation no one had ever finished.

The first time anyone noticed the organ grinder was the morning he appeared on the corner of Sixth and Ash with nothing but a monkey, a violin case, and a brass bell tied to a rope around his waist. No permit, no paperwork, no prior mention in the city’s endless parade of eccentrics or sanctioned performers. He simply stood there, the monkey perched on his shoulder like a mischievous thought, and began to play.

The monkey clapped tiny hands to a rhythm no one else could hear, its face a mixture of boredom and theatrical concentration. The music was neither classical nor jazz—it was something else, a hybrid of forgotten lullabies and war cries, the kind of sound that made pedestrians pause not out of curiosity, but out of a primal need to remember something lost. A woman in a fur coat stopped mid-stride, her face softening into a smile she hadn’t allowed herself in years. A boy with asthma, usually too weak to notice the world, found himself breathing in time with the tune.

The organ grinder never looked up, never acknowledged the crowd forming. He was not there to impress or to entertain in the usual sense. He was there to remind—to stir something beneath the surface of the city’s carefully curated indifference. The monkey, meanwhile, seemed to understand the performance fully. It would sometimes reach down and adjust the grinder’s sleeve, or nod sagely at passersby as if confirming some secret truth about them.

By noon, the crowd had grown thick enough to slow traffic. No one asked for change. No one asked for identification. They listened, they breathed, they remembered. A man who’d lost his daughter to a hospital fire stood in the sunlight and wept, not from sorrow, but from relief—she had loved monkeys. She would have laughed at the sight of this one.

As the hour passed, the organ grinder’s music shifted. It grew softer, then louder, then quieter still, as if following some internal logic that only the monkey understood. By the time he finished, the street was silent. No one spoke. No one moved. It was as if the entire city had been suspended for a breath, waiting for something to return.

The monkey gave one last, deliberate clap. The organ grinder picked up his case, fastened the brass bell around his waist once more, and walked away. No one followed. No one asked where he was going. The city had changed, just slightly, just enough. And that was all.

On the morning of April 23rd, Mayor Eleanor Voss read the headline twice before the meaning fully settled in: “City Hall Adopts Mandatory Laughter Policy.” It was the kind of phrase that should have been set off with italics, or perhaps a note in parentheses explaining that, yes, it was entirely in earnest.

She sat back in her chair, her fingers tapping the armrest in slow, deliberate rhythm. The headline had been accompanied by a photo of the council room the previous night, where, to celebrate the passage of the policy—after much deliberation and several rounds of interpretive dance—each member had been seen clapping one hand over their mouth while laughing into the other.

According to the article, the new law required city employees to emit at least thirty seconds of genuine laughter each day, measured via biometric wristbands distributed to all municipal staff. The rationale, as stated in the mayor’s speech, was twofold: to improve morale and to create a more welcoming atmosphere for the city's many residents, who, according to a recent survey, ranked “feeling joy while waiting for a permit” somewhere between “unlikely” and “laughable.”

Eleanor turned to the memo on her desk, written by the same deputy who had assured her the policy would be “fun.” The memo detailed that City Hall had entered into a partnership with a startup based in Brooklyn, which specialized in what they called “Affective Output Optimization.” The company’s technology supposedly tracked laughter levels in real-time, sending gentle electric pulses through the wristband if a mandated session of chuckling had not occurred.

The mayor sighed. She remembered a time when red tape meant something. Now it was replaced with something she imagined might be described as yellow laughter.

Still, she had signed the bill. The city had adopted it. And if it meant that every time a resident came in for a zoning change or license renewal, they would be met with a chorus of giggles and guffaws, then so be it.

She glanced at her assistant, who had entered quietly and was now standing by the door, trying to suppress a smile.

“Did you hear the one about the city planner who walked into a bank?” the assistant said.

“I’m waiting,” Eleanor replied.

“He couldn’t get a loan because the teller said he lacked the proper form of amusement.”

Eleanor looked at the clock. 9:17 a.m. Exactly twenty-three seconds until her mandatory laughter quota began.

She smiled. Then laughed, slowly at first, then with increasing volume, until her head was thrown back and tears were forming at the corners of her eyes.

Harold P. Glickman, editorial director of Houghton Mifflin's contemporary literature wing, is a man of modest tastes and exacting standards—though the two often conflict, in his case. His office, a narrow room wedged between the accounting department and the warehouse for unread galleys, contains precisely twenty-two books. All of them, he insists, were selected for their "profound readability." None of them, to his knowledge, were ever read. Harold does not count this a failure. He counts it a quiet victory over entropy.

Each morning, Harold arrives at the office promptly at 9:07 a.m. (He believes in punctuality, but not servitude to clocks). He brews a pot of coffee that no one else drinks. It is strong, black, and brewed from beans roasted on the third floor of the Houghton Mifflin building, where the company’s internal cafe operates under the banner *The Literary Cup*. The barista, Ms. Rafferty, has written a chapbook on the symbolism of espresso foam, which she occasionally attempts to sell to the interns. They pretend not to notice.

Harold’s job, officially, is to oversee acquisitions in the contemporary literature department, though it is understood within the company that this means, in practical terms, reading manuscripts submitted by authors who are either unknown or insistent. Each week, a stack of proposals arrives, labeled not with the titles of the books, but with the names of the authors, in parentheses, like this: *(Mabel Wren: The Whale of Little Falls)* or *(Julian Voss: The Ghost Who Didn’t Die – Twice)*. These are sorted into three piles: “Consider,” “Wait,” and “Burn.” The last pile is Harold’s favorite. It is the most honest.

On Mondays, Harold reads aloud from “Consider” manuscripts to a parrot named Reginald, who occupies a perch above his filing cabinet and is believed to have once worked in the poetry division. Reginald does not judge the quality of the work—he judges the rhythm. If he tilts his head or squawks twice, the manuscript goes into “Burn.” If he remains silent, Harold considers it a pass.

Recently, a manuscript titled *The Almanac of Small Disasters* arrived on Harold’s desk. It was sent by a woman named Clara Moreau, listed as residing in a place called “Maple Hollow,” which does not appear on any map he owns. The manuscript contained only twelve stories, each exactly 312 words long. Each was narrated by a different character, none of whom were the same, yet all of whom experienced some form of minor catastrophe—lost keys, forgotten engagements, misplaced letters. The tone was melancholic, but not despairing. It was, in a way Harold found almost disturbingly rare in modern writing, *gracious*.

He read the first story twice. Then, for reasons he could not explain, he read it a third.

THE first sign that Dr. Marnie Thistle had gone permanently off the rails was when she removed her shoes and stood in the center of the biology lab, humming “On the Road Again” while holding a vial of genetically modified yeast labeled *Saccharomyces Sentimentalis*.  

She’d spent the prior week convinced the organism was composing limericks. This was, according to Dr. Thistle, not unheard of among postmodern microorganisms. “They’ve been known to evolve metaphors,” she told the graduate student who had once admired her but now wore a nervous smile. “You just need to know where to look—cell membranes are like parentheses. Mitochondria are the punchline.”

Colleagues had started leaving her lab quietly after department meetings, citing “extreme fatigue” or sudden family obligations. Even the janitor, a man whose sole ambition was to avoid interaction, began closing doors twice in succession to ensure privacy.

Dr. Thistle, meanwhile, had begun publishing in obscure journals with names like *The Quarterly Journal of Irreversible Inquiry* and *Biology & Beyond: Speculations, Mutations, and Other Forms of Inquiry*. Her latest paper argued that photosynthesis was essentially a metaphor for regret.

The university’s ethics board was in deliberation. The department chair, Dr. Hargrove, was quoted in the internal newsletter as saying, “Marnie’s research is... unconventional. Let’s say it walks a tightrope between genius and nonsense. But until the board rules otherwise, she remains in good standing.” 

What Dr. Hargrove didn’t say aloud, but which everyone knew, was that if Dr. Thistle had gone off the deep end, she was going in style. Her lectures had become theatrical. One afternoon, she appeared in a lab coat painted like a zebra and lectured on chromosomal migration using interpretive dance. Students were required to write essays in verse. One of them later remarked that it felt like attending the lecture of a philosopher, but one who had somehow mistaken philosophy for microbiology.  

Still, the students loved her. They hung on every word, every gesture, every twitch of her expressive hands. They found her inspiring, even if they couldn’t always follow her. After all, she had once taken the entire class to a midnight showing of *2001: A Space Odyssey*, followed by a seminar on the biological implications of the monolith.  

But now, the rumors had shifted. Some whispered that Dr. Thistle had discovered a strain of algae that could produce existential despair. Others believed she’d invented a language spoken only by tardigrades. The most alarming theory—spread quietly in hallways over coffee and lukewarm pastries—was that she had, in fact, stopped sleeping, and that this lack of sleep had caused her mind to blur the line between science and poetry.

And then, one morning, the lab was found empty save for the vial of *Saccharomyces Sentimentalis*, now labeled *Waiting for Godot*. A single whiteboard read:

> “I am not missing. I have simply moved closer to the truth.”

And beneath that, in large, looping script:

> “If you must search for me, check the place where science forgets it is dreaming.”

The first time I heard her speak in public, it was at a symposium for avant-garde philosophers, a room filled mostly with men in tweed whispering about axioms and absurdity, and she walked in like a gust of wind had just decided to take the form of a human being. Her name was Clara Wrenn, and she had written a book titled *On the Ontology of Quotation Marks*, which, as far as I could tell, was either a profound meditation on language or a cruel joke. I didn’t know which at the time, and I still don’t.

Clara wore a black dress that looked like it had been tailored from the shadows of a cathedral’s arches, and her hair—short, precise, unapologetic—seemed to defy gravity in the kind of way that only someone utterly comfortable with their own presence could manage. She began her talk with a question: “If I say ‘meaning,’ am I saying meaning or merely quoting it?” A pause, then another, longer one, before the audience realized she wasn’t going to answer.

The lecture was a performance. She moved through the room like a ghost, her voice calm and rhythmic, as though she were reciting poetry or reading a spell aloud. At one point, she quoted Wittgenstein, then unquoted him. Then she quoted herself, then denied having done so. She played the crowd like a tuning fork, striking nerves with every carefully chosen inflection.

By the end, half the people in the room were scribbling furiously in notebooks, and the other half were staring at her like she had removed the floor beneath their understanding of reality. I didn’t write anything. I just stared, too, but not in confusion. I had the unsettling feeling that she had seen into me and left nothing behind except a question mark.

In the middle of a perfectly ordinary Tuesday, the National Weather Service announced that the sky had officially changed color. Not in a poetic sense—like “blue turned to gray” or “sunshine became melancholy.” No, the sky had become, according to official instruments, the precise hue of a used coffee filter soaked in yesterday’s dishwater. They named it Condition Ozone-9. Nobody had ever heard of Condition Ozone-9 before, but it was described in such technical detail—particulate ratios, spectral absorption, refractive indices—that the public accepted it without question. 

By 9:03 a.m., the sky remained the same shade, and the sun, which had once been yellow, was now a very pale, watery green. Birds stopped flying over the city. Dogs refused to walk outside unless led by leashes. Children asked their parents if the world was ending and were sternly reminded that “the world does *not* end.”

At 10:15, someone in the Department of Agriculture declared that no food should be consumed unless boiled twice, once in salt and once in vinegar. Grocery stores sold out of both in under forty minutes.

By noon, television hosts began wearing protective goggles. They also started speaking in measured, flat tones. One anchor, mid-broadcast, forgot his name and was replaced by a man from the weather channel who read from a script titled “Calm and Assured Responses to Global Uncertainty.”

Meanwhile, a man in Ohio named Harold, who worked part-time as a librarian and mostly as a janitor at a local community college, noticed that his cat had begun typing furiously on the family keyboard. Not literally—Harold was no stranger to feline mischief—but the cat’s behavior suggested purpose. He left the cat alone, unsure whether to laugh or cry. The next day, the cat had written an entire thesis on the philosophical implications of Condition Ozone-9 in Postmodern Architecture. It was published online the same afternoon.

By Thursday, a global consensus emerged that the sky’s new color was symbolic. Some thought it represented the collapse of trust. Others believed it symbolized the end of privacy. A few claimed it was an omen of a new era of transparency, or at least a warning that things were getting clearer—if you knew how to look.

But no one could look directly at it without blinking.

The parrot had always claimed to be a tax accountant, but no one had ever seen him do taxes, and certainly not for any of the zookeepers. Still, he insisted. “I deduct my parrotseed,” he’d squawk whenever asked about his clients. “I do deductions and credits—oh yes, I’m a specialist in depreciation, baby!” He wore a tiny eyeglass, one lens missing, perched on the bridge of his beak. His name was Oscar, though no one remembered if that was his birth name or a name given by a child visitor in the 1980s who had once written it in permanent marker on a discarded cage tag.

Oscar lived in the back corner of the Aviary Annex, a forgotten wing of the city zoo that had long since gone defunct. Now it served mostly as a storage unit for retired animals—birds with clipped wings, snakes with too many teeth, the occasional lion who had grown tired of performing. Oscar’s enclosure was a repurposed filing cabinet, its drawers labeled in a mix of Latin, Swahili, and numbers. Visitors rarely came near anymore, and those who did usually mistook him for a stuffed prop from a failed exhibit.

But Oscar worked diligently, even if no one believed him. Each morning, he sat cross-legged on the top drawer, his plumage ruffled like a suit of feathers, and pecked at a ledger with a bent pen. The pages were filled with names like “Captain Cucuzzi,” “Lady Macaroon,” and “Mr. Whiskerbottom,” all clients he supposedly represented. He would mutter to himself in a voice like rusted gears: “Section 171-A, subsection 6-B—carryforward losses, capital gains, oh, what a mess.” And yet, when asked whether he had ever filed a real return, he’d snap, “Who needs the IRS when you’ve got me?”

One Tuesday, something changed. Oscar hadn’t shown up for breakfast. The keeper, a woman named Mira, checked the cabinet. Nothing. No pen, no ledger, no parrot. She opened the drawer slowly, her shadow stretching across the floor. Inside, neatly stacked, were dozens of colorful tax forms, stamped with the seal of the Avian Revenue Bureau (ARB), a fictional agency only Oscar seemed to recognize. The top form read:

TO: HONEST AMERICAN BIRDS  
FROM: OSCAR M. PARROT CPA  
TAX YEAR: 2012  
SUBJECT: CLAIM FOR FEATHER LOSS DUE TO INFLATIONARY WEATHER CONDITIONS  

She smiled, though it didn’t reach her eyes. Oscar wasn’t missing—he had simply moved the office. Somewhere, in a cage, a tree, maybe even a mailbox, the parrot tax accountant was out there, still working, still claiming, still adding. Mira pocketed one of the forms. She’d frame it. Next to the bird feed.

THE first time I heard the phrase “Crisis of the Day” spoken aloud was at a faculty meeting in the fall of ’72. Dr. Halberton, chair of the English Department, delivered it with all the solemnity of someone announcing a national emergency. “We’re seeing a Crisis of the Day phenomenon on campus,” he said, tapping his notes as if they might burst into flames. “Students are no longer content with one crisis at a time. They demand a fresh one every Monday.”

I sat in the back of the room, chewing on the inside of my lip, thinking how strange it was that crises, once rare and heavy things like wars and revolutions, had now been reduced to a weekly routine—like housekeeping or flossing.

Later that week, the campus newspaper confirmed it. Monday brought the announcement of Budget Cut Brenda, followed by Tuesday’s Student Housing Shortage Sally. Wednesday featured the unveiling of Academic Freedom Fred, and Thursday the return of Sexual Harassment Hank with a vengeance. Friday was for protest and reflection, and Saturday and Sunday were reserved for recovery. Or so we hoped.

By noon on the following Monday, I had been assigned the dubious task of handling Crisis of the Day for the Philosophy Department. My predecessor had retired suddenly, citing “existential fatigue.” I had no training for it, of course. The job consisted mostly of reading crisis updates, writing press statements, and ensuring the department did not become the center of any particular storm.

On my first day, I opened my inbox to find a message titled simply: *New Crisis: Coffee Table Bob*. 

I stared at the screen for a while. Then I walked down the hall to the faculty lounge, where Dr. Halberton sipped from a thermos labeled *Ethics in Action* and Dr. Lasky argued with a photocopier. I said, “There’s a new Crisis.”

Dr. Lasky looked up. “Which one?”

“Coffee Table Bob.”

He blinked. “That’s not a person.”

“No,” I agreed. “But apparently it’s a crisis.”

“I assume it refers to the fact that no one can agree on how to sit near the table in the common room?”

“That’s not noted in the briefing.”

Dr. Halberton sighed and lowered his thermos. “Then I suppose it’s time to meet with the faculty and discuss the philosophical implications of a coffee table gone awry.” 

He smiled grimly. “After all, if it’s a Crisis of the Day, it’s also a Crisis of Thought.”

THE PROBLEM OF THE PRESIDENTIAL DOG

It began with a bark.

Not just any bark, mind you, but one that split the morning calm of the White House lawn like a shot, waking Secret Service agents mid-sip, startling birds from cherry trees, and prompting the First Lady to pause in mid-step as she exited the East Wing, her silk scarf fluttering with the urgency of scandal.

For weeks, the Kennedys had insisted that the presidential dog—a collie named Mac, acquired from a ranch in Texas with a vague claim to royal lineage—was perfectly behaved. This, despite the fact that Mac had once leaped through a window during a visit to London, mistaking it for a portal to open pasture. His presence in the White House was meant to symbolize the wholesome, all-American image they wished to project: sturdy, loyal, and quietly noble.

But as spring turned into summer, it became clear that Mac was neither quiet nor noble. He barked at passing motorcades, barked at photographers, barked at the moon. He barked at nothing, and he barked at everything. It was a sound that defied reason and training alike.

The Secret Service, long accustomed to presidential unpredictability, took the barking as a warning sign. Could it be a coded message from the animal world? Were the barks timed to match Morse code, or perhaps the frequency of a foreign broadcast?

The White House staff, meanwhile, divided into two factions: those who believed Mac was simply bored and in need of stimulation, and those who suspected he had been bred for espionage, perhaps trained by CIA handlers to detect hidden microphones or suspicious silhouettes.

The First Lady, usually composed, grew visibly unsettled. She had once laughed off the idea of a dog as a political liability. “Dogs are loyal,” she had said. “They don’t play games.” But now, during dinner parties and state functions, Mac would fix guests with a stare, then let loose a volley of barks that could only be interpreted as judgment.

Even the President’s closest advisors were not immune. The National Security Council convened behind closed doors to debate the implications of a canine with an agenda. Was the dog responding to unseen threats? Could he sense the tension of a divided nation? Or worse—had he been compromised?

Then came the incident with the senator from Maine.

During a private meeting in the Treaty Room, the dog leapt onto the desk, scattering memos and overturning a pitcher of iced tea. He barked, low and menacing, directly at the senator, who left the room pale and shaken. That night, the senator announced his withdrawal from a key Senate committee—no explanation, only a cryptic statement about feeling “unduly targeted.”

Inside the White House, whispers took root. Was Mac protecting the presidency? Warning of treachery? Or was he, as one staffer joked, merely a mad dog with a taste for drama?

No one yet knew. But the barking continued, persistent and precise, like a signal from another world—one where loyalty was measured not in speeches or votes, but in how loud and often you barked when the time was right.

The new Vice President of the United States is a man named Reginald Thistlethwaite, and it is widely believed in certain upper-atmosphere think tanks that he was born in a year that did not yet exist. Some say 1929. Others suggest 1964 or perhaps a month that fell out of the calendar during a period of confusion. But the truth, as far as anyone in the public can tell, is that he entered the world under a sign not mentioned in any horoscope section, and spent his childhood in a town where all the clocks were set to different time zones. 

He is 67 years old, or claims to be, depending on whether you ask his campaign manager, his tailor, or his daughter, who is currently studying astrophysics at a university known primarily for its excellent coffee shop and vague admissions standards. The Vice President does not appear to sleep. In official photographs, he is consistently positioned three inches to the left of any actual light source, suggesting either a deliberate pose or the effects of prolonged exposure to fluorescent lighting. 

His favorite color is chartreuse, though in a recent press conference, he was observed wearing a chartreuse scarf paired with a suit that was approximately 82% black and 18% regret. The Secret Service keeps a running tally of the number of times he taps his fingers on any surface in a span of ten minutes—a count that has exceeded 700 in certain high-stress situations involving tax code amendments or the accidental importation of foreign avocados.

Reginald Thistlethwaite has never been seen with a drink of any kind in his hand, yet the smell of aged whiskey lingers around him like a forgotten anecdote. He speaks in complete paragraphs, though often without a subject, and his speeches contain entire sentences that do not follow from the ones before them. It is unclear whether this is a stylistic choice or a neurological one. 

During the transition of power, he was photographed standing in the Lincoln Memorial with his back to the statue of Honest Abe, staring directly at a reflection in a fountain where, according to multiple witnesses, no fountain existed. When asked about this later, he responded that it was not a reflection, but a “projection of moral clarity,” and that Lincoln, were he alive, would have approved of his policy on the regulation of national hummingbird habitats. 

The press corps watches him with a wary affection, like people who have bought a slightly defective watch and hope it might someday tick correctly. They quote him. They do not trust him. They are unsure whether he is a character from a satire, a satire of a character, or a character who forgot the plot.

Not the kind of misprint that causes consternation among guests who can't choose between the saffron risotto and the saffron risotto—no, this was something subtler, something with consequences. At the opening night of La Maison du Miel, the new restaurant in the twelfth arrondissement that promised to redefine French dining, the waiter handed each diner a menu bearing the following ominous line: Entrée: Coq au Vin, à l’ancienne, ou Coq à la Vin, à la moderne. The comma had gone missing in the middle of *Coq au Vin*, and thus the entrée became something altogether other. It read as if it were two choices, rather than one refined dish. The mistake was subtle, but it carried weight—like a misplaced semicolon in the constitution or a typo in a love letter that changes everything. 

By the time the first course arrived—veal sweetbreads prepared *à la mode* of the chef, served in a cream sauce with a reduction of burgundy—the confusion had already begun to fester. Some patrons, interpreting the menu as a menu of possibilities, ordered the *Coq à la Vin*, a dish that didn’t exist outside of grammatical curiosity. Others, more astute, assumed it was a clever play on the classics, a joke for the cognoscenti. The kitchen, meanwhile, remained blissfully unaware of the linguistic schism unfolding in the dining room.

But the damage had been done. Word spread through the tables. A journalist from *Le Monde* began taking notes with a look of mild bewilderment, as if the whole thing were somehow both absurd and profound. A visiting diplomat from the Ministry of Culture asked to see the owner. And so, minutes after the first bite of sweetbread, the identity of the meal—and by extension, the identity of the restaurant itself—was called into question.

This was, of course, just the beginning. The missing comma had unleashed something beyond food criticism: a crisis of meaning, a fracture in the delicate architecture of language and expectation. How could anyone be sure what they were eating if the words on the page could no longer be trusted?

The owner, a former poet who had traded meter for mise en place, responded with the poise of someone who had always known this moment was coming. He stepped into the dining room, his face unreadable, and with a single flourish, declared the entire evening an *œuvre d’art culinaire*. “Let us,” he said in a measured tone, “interpret the menu in whatever way inspires us.”

And so, the diners did. Some chose the classic, others the modern. Some chose both, and some, perhaps, chose neither. The meal continued, and the world changed, just a little, beneath the flicker of candlelight."

THE idea that human beings have ever been truly free is a charming delusion, like believing that gravity is optional, or that a well-placed wink can cancel a law. Yet it persists, like the belief that a sufficiently large cheese wheel can float a house. Freedom, as far as anyone can determine, is an idea invented by people who were not yet aware of the extent to which they were already bound. The earliest records indicate that even in the most liberated of early civilizations—say, the Sumerians or the Egyptians—people were still, at base, either working, being ordered to work, or dying. So it’s not freedom in the popular sense that interests me, but rather the spectacle of modern man straining against invisible walls, convinced he’s breaking through them when in fact he’s only hitting the same glass ceiling with different shoes.

Consider, for example, the rise of the “personal brand.” In years past, a person might have had a job, a name, perhaps a reputation. Today, a person must also have a brand. This is not metaphorical; it is literal. You must market yourself. You must align with values. You must be seen, understood, remembered. It’s not enough to exist anymore—you must represent something, preferably something marketable. You must be a platform, a portfolio, a proposition. You must be, in essence, a curated version of yourself, optimized for visibility and consumption. One might reasonably ask: who are these consumers, and what are they consuming? Mostly, it seems, other people. And not in the old, casual way of passing by a stranger on the street and feeling briefly curious about their life. No, the modern consumer of the human brand wants to be fed, regularly and reliably, bits of identity, lifestyle, aspiration. They want proof that you’re awake, aware, authentic—and preferably wearing something interesting.

This is where the illusion comes in. The idea that by managing your self-presentation you become more powerful, more in control. That by choosing your aesthetic and your narrative, you are, somehow, free. But in truth, the brand is not yours—it is the algorithm’s. It is the culture’s. It is the invisible hand that has decided for you what you should desire, how you should dress, how you should feel about your job, your body, your thoughts. You are not in control. You are a performance, and the audience is hungry.

The mayor’s press secretary announced it in the usual way—by mistake. She was reading off a list of upcoming civic projects, the kind that sound ambitious but amount to repaving the same potholes three times, when she slipped and said it: “And finally, we’re thrilled to unveil the new Urban Harmony Initiative, designed to foster cooperation between the Department of Recreation and the city’s growing population of sentient pigeons.” The crowd laughed at first. People did that—laughter being the easiest reaction when you didn’t want to scream. Then someone asked a question, and the laughter died.

It began, as these things often do, with a bird named Marigold. She was not the first pigeon to speak—there had been whispers, a few strange coos that sounded almost like vowels—but Marigold was the first to say “crumbs” in full, coherent English while pecking at a discarded slice of sourdough outside the Central Library. The librarian, a man named Haskins who had memorized every edition of *Birdsong Monthly*, reported it, naturally. He assumed a prank. But Marigold spoke again the next day, and the next. Then came others. Flocks with grievances. A pair nesting in the bell tower who called for better waste disposal in residential areas. One bird, a large one with a blue crest, started demanding sidewalks. It wasn’t long before the city had to assign someone just to listen.

Now, three years later, they’ve built a pavilion near City Hall, all glass and steel and pigeon-proof wire, where officials and avian representatives meet weekly to discuss traffic patterns, trash collection, and the controversial proposal to paint the courthouse in a shade of brown that resembles a nesting site. The pigeons vote. The pigeons protest. The pigeons write op-eds for the *Daily Herald* under pseudonyms like “Skywatcher 303.”

You might think it’s a joke, but then you’d be wrong. The birds are serious. They’re also dirty and loud and allergic to change. They’ve unionized. They’ve formed factions. There’s the Loft Liberals, the Nest Nativists, the Fly-By-Night Republicans. And yes, the mayor does have a pigeon advisor now, a sleek white bird named Chancellor who sits on a cushioned perch at council meetings and makes his opinions known through a series of deliberate, guttural clucks and the occasional hissed sentence.

Tonight, Chancellor will deliver his keynote address on urban sprawl and the ethics of feeding wild birds. The mayor’s office is preparing a response. Some people are preparing to riot. And somewhere, a flock is circling the old water tower, waiting for the signal.

"Dr. Ellery Tarnish has been unwell. It is whispered that he is unwell in the kind of way that whispers cling to men who have spent decades at the center of invisible wars. His reputation as the mind behind the Strategic Algorithm, the predictive model said to anticipate regional shifts with eerie precision, preceded him like a ghost. He was never a soldier, nor a general, but in boardrooms and backchannels, his name was spoken with the reverence usually reserved for those who shape history from its underbelly. Yet lately, there have been absences—meetings canceled without explanation, briefings postponed until silence hung too thickly in the halls where his influence once hummed. The leaks began soon after.

Not the kind of leaks that make the papers, but the subtle ones, the kind that arrive folded twice and tucked into diplomatic pouches. Information—strategic, classified, sometimes absurdly so—seeped into places it had no business. A Russian think tank cited data that mirrored classified U.S. projections on energy trade flows. A French analyst, citing unnamed sources, broke the precise timeline of a planned infrastructure investment in the Balkans before the committee had even convened. Each leak bore the unmistakable stamp of Tarnish’s old methodology: elegant, minimal in footprint, devastating in effect.

His colleagues are divided. Some believe he is under duress, coerced in ways that no one dares ask about. Others suggest he has simply grown weary, that decades of parsing human conflict with mathematical rigor have dulled him to the chaos he once predicted. But there is a third faction, smaller, quieter, whose voices are heard mostly in the margins of memos and off-record briefings. These are the ones who say Dr. Tarnish is not leaking. He is *correcting*. Adjusting the algorithm mid-course, recalibrating the variables to something no one yet understands.

The latest incident happened last Thursday. During a closed-door session at Langley, the Director presented a report on cyber threats emanating from Southeast Asia. The data was comprehensive, the projections alarming. But after the meeting, it emerged that the same data had appeared simultaneously on a secure academic server in Norway, accessible only to a handful of scholars. The coincidence was too clean. Someone had fed the data to the outside world—but not randomly. Only the key indicators remained, stripped of noise, arranged in a pattern that suggested intent rather than accident.

And now, the question remains: Did Dr. Ellery Tarnish fall? Or did he, at long last, rise?"

At precisely 3:14 a.m., the moon blinked twice and vanished behind a shelf of cirrus clouds. This was the cue. Somewhere beneath the city—deeper than subways, deeper than secrets—the first of the machines stirred.

They had been lying dormant since the last blackout, rusted in their niches along the concrete arteries of the underground. Now, with the flick of a ghost switch somewhere in Brooklyn, they began to turn. At first only a low whine, a vibration felt in the soles of the feet by a few sleepless souls walking home from the 3 a.m. diner. Then the hum became a drone, a rising crescendo that vibrated glass panes and shook the teeth of old men fast asleep in their recliners. 

By 3:22 a.m., the machines had surfaced in the alleys behind the bodegas and laundromats. They were humanoid, but wrong—wires like veins under synthetic skin, joints that articulated with the wet crunch of bone, eyes that glowed faintly green in the dark. They moved in unison, silent as snowfall, their metal fingers tapping Morse code on the brick walls. Their message was universal: *We are returning.*

Across the city, birds took flight in confused flocks. The pigeons, particularly, understood the language of the machines better than humans did. They wheeled in tight spirals over the rooftops, squawking warnings the people below dismissed as just another Tuesday.

In East Harlem, a woman named Mabel Rosa awoke to the sound of something heavy rolling across her fire escape. She stood at the window, a mug of lukewarm tea in her hand, and watched as the first machine climbed over the railing like a spider made of steel. It paused, then raised a hand and knocked once, deliberately, on her door.

Inside the building, the elderly tenants stirred. Some reached for their canes, others for their Bibles. But Mabel knew better. She lived across the hall from the old man who had worked in the subway tunnels before the city buried them all. He had told her stories about the things that slept beneath the city, waiting for the day when the power would fail long enough to bring them home.

She opened the door slowly. The machine looked at her, its eye lenses pulsing amber. It held out a small, glowing cube. Not a weapon. A message.

Mabel took it, and the machine stepped back into the night.

By 3:31 a.m., the machines had spread to the Financial District. Wall Street, once the beating heart of human commerce, was now the first front line in a silent war that had been brewing for decades. And by the time the sun rose, the entire city would know.

THE PRESIDENT WAS FISHING FOR METAPHORS the morning the satellite went silent over the South Pacific. He sat on the edge of the Rose Garden, fly rod in hand, though no water stretched before him but the manicured grass and the marble steps of the Lincoln Memorial in the distance. The Secret Service agents nearby watched with the kind of stoicism reserved for presidents who pretend to fish while the world waits to hear what they really think. His line was a spool of metaphor, he told them once, when someone asked why he did it. It’s about casting doubt into certainty, reeling in what truths we can before the tide swallows them whole. They nodded, said nothing, and kept the sun off his back.

Inside the Oval Office, the National Security Council was already debating whether the signal loss was a glitch or a declaration of intent. Analysts speculated on rogue satellites, solar flares, deliberate jamming, but the President had only his rod and the weight of the words he’d rehearsed in silence for years. That morning, he had not yet spoken. He cast the line again, watching the bobber float on an imaginary current.

By noon, it became clear the silence would not break. A full-sized delegation from the European Union arrived, bearing a formal inquiry wrapped in velvet and lined with questions. They stood under the trees outside Blair House, waiting for a response that would shape the next decade. Meanwhile, the President walked through the East Wing, greeting schoolchildren touring the Diplomatic Reception Room, shaking their hands, smiling like a man who believed in the fiction he sold for a living.

At four o’clock, a young intern handed him a note. *The satellite remains offline. Requesting clarification on intent.* He read it twice, then folded it into a paper crane and dropped it into a goldfish bowl on the mantel. The fish swam lazily in circles, unburdened by geopolitics.

Later, he convened a private session in the Cabinet Room. No cameras. No leaks. The men and women of power sat in their seats, waiting for the speech that might change history. Instead, he lit a candle at the center of the table and said, “Let’s talk about what happens when the light goes out.” They listened, as always, not knowing whether he meant the satellite, or them. Or maybe, they hoped, himself.

THE NEW GALLERY  

It’s true that no one really liked the new gallery, but then again, no one ever really liked *any* new gallery. They all started with a kind of forced enthusiasm, the kind that comes from having too much money and not enough taste. It was all about the name—the name that wasn’t a name, the name that was a question or maybe a statement—New Gallery, *The* New Gallery, “A New Gallery.” The way it was pronounced made people roll their eyes, not in disapproval exactly, but in recognition. They knew where they were headed.  

It opened in a part of town that had recently stopped being fashionable in the way that fashion stops being fashionable—it simply shifted. The old café that used to draw poets and insomniacs had been replaced by a bakery that sold bread in the shape of famous artists’ heads, and the bookshop had moved into the upstairs apartment and became a bookshop that didn’t sell books. They sold interpretations.  

The owner of the New Gallery had once been a curator, though no one could remember which museum. He’d written a series of essays on the “death of representation” and spent a weekend at a remote cabin somewhere in the mountains translating the same essay into French. He returned with a better tan and a slightly different accent.  

The first exhibit was titled “Objects in the Mirror Are Closer Than They Appear.” It was mostly sculptures and photographs, and one installation in the back room that required visitors to wear headphones and stand perfectly still for at least ten minutes. If you stood still longer, the gallery promised, you might begin to see things.  

People came. They stood in the front, nodded, took photos without smiling, and left. Some of them never came back. Others returned to see if the installation would tell them something different the second time around.  

On the wall near the coat check, the artist had placed a sign: *Do not adjust your head. Adjust the angle of your gaze.*  

It was unclear if this was advice or a warning.

Senator Eliza Whitmore’s recent resignation has left a vacuum not only in the Senate chamber but also in the intricate web of patronage that surrounds Washington politics like ivy on a marble column. Her absence has prompted a flurry of speculation regarding the dozens of lesser-known, yet strategically vital, administrative positions under her jurisdiction—positions that for years were filled not with a nod to the merit rolls but according to a delicate balance of gratitude, obligation, and the occasional well-timed birthday card. Now, with her desk emptied of correspondence, her office stripped of the trinkets and tokens of allegiance (including a particularly garish porcelain squirrel gifted by the Iowa delegation), the question on everyone’s lips is: Who will inherit the spoils?

Among the most coveted of these vacancies is the post of Deputy Director of the National Arboretum—a role that sounds innocuous enough but carries a surprising amount of influence, given the symbolic weight of the trees. It is said the current acting director, Dr. Harold Linwood, has kept a running tally of every sapling planted during the administration, noting species, location, and political donor. His successor will inherit not only the oaks and maples but also the quiet power of green gestures—diplomatic arbors planted for visiting heads of state, groves dedicated to retiring senators, and, most importantly, the rare white-barked birches that line the walk to the West Wing, a legacy project begun by a beloved but departed predecessor.

Meanwhile, the interim director of the Office of Cultural Preservation has reportedly received three discreet calls from hopefuls vying for the Arboretum post. The first is Professor Eleanor Voss, a soft-spoken academic with a doctorate in dendrochronology and a reputation for turning bureaucratic meetings into lectures on the carbon isotopes in ancient wood. The second is Marcus Delaney, a former campaign manager to Senator Whitmore, who claims to have been her "green conscience." The third is simply known as "The Botanist," an anonymous figure said to have once revived a dying camellia in the State Department’s Rose Garden with a whispered prayer and a bottle of distilled moonlight.

All of them, of course, are watching. Not merely the Arboretum itself, but each other—and the man who might tip the scales. That would be Congressman James Pritchard, a man not known for his love of flora, but whose district includes the largest contiguous forest in the region, and who has thus far remained conspicuously silent.

As autumn deepens and the leaves turn to whispers on the wind, the Washington of trees is waiting.

At precisely 3:14 a.m. on a Tuesday, the National Weather Service issued a routine advisory regarding a patch of low pressure over Lake Superior. Unbeknownst to the meteorologists, this advisory, printed in standard-issue font, had triggered a cascading malfunction in the automated irrigation systems of three states—Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Michigan. The glitch manifested in the form of an overwhelming surge of water directed not toward fields of corn and soybean, but instead toward the interiors of homes, businesses, and, most inexplicably, libraries.

By 3:41 a.m., residents awoke to the sound of trickling water from ceiling tiles, the subtle gurgle of hidden pipes now singing full-throated choruses. In Madison, a librarian discovered an entire shelf of Victorian novels submerged beneath inches of chlorinated lake water. In Duluth, a diner was forced to cancel breakfast service when a flock of geese, presumed to be migratory strays, waded into the flooded dining area and demanded toast with beak-like insistence.

And yet, the real disturbance was not in the water—but in the silence it left behind.

By 4:12 a.m., every radio in the Midwest had gone dark. Not dead. Not jammed. Quiet. Engineers at stations in Milwaukee, St. Paul, and Detroit were baffled. No signals, no static, not even the faint hum of electrical interference. Just… quiet. It wasn’t until 4:33 a.m., when a retired disc jockey in Eau Claire managed to tune his old AM radio to a dead frequency, that he picked up something strange: a voice—not human, not machine, but something caught in between. “They’re waiting,” it said, before the transmission collapsed into a sigh of static.

In the same hour, a man named Reginald Haskins, director of the Great Lakes Regional Waterworks Authority, found himself unable to close the file labeled *Project Mermaid* on his office computer. It had never existed before, yet there it was, open and humming, filled with diagrams of underwater tunnels leading nowhere, and photographs of fish with human eyes.

By 5:04 a.m., the water had stopped flowing. The skies cleared. Radios stayed silent.

Reginald poured himself a second coffee, sat down, and opened the file fully. A message blinked onscreen: *The system is listening.*

The Vice-President’s pet alligator was found wandering the halls of the West Wing the morning after the address on energy policy. According to Secret Service surveillance tapes, the creature—named Lucinda—was first spotted near the Lincoln Sitting Room, cloaked in a bathrobe borrowed, presumably, from the Vice-President’s own collection. The footage shows her waddling with surprising grace, clutching a half-eaten muffin in one clawed hand and a briefing book stamped *CONFIDENTIAL: Solar Subsidy Proposals* in the other.

Lucinda had been a gift from the Governor of Louisiana for services rendered during the oil crisis of '78. She was kept in a custom-built vivarium behind the second-floor solarium, where the Vice-President conducted weekly strategy sessions with the National Energy Council. Her presence was intended to inspire a sense of gravitas, or perhaps a quiet intimidation, though the effect had grown increasingly surreal as the years passed. Staff referred to her as “the moral compass” of the energy policy team—though not in his hearing.

By the time the incident was discovered, Lucinda had made her way to the Oval Office, where the President was reportedly mid-sentence about the future of nuclear fission. According to eyewitness accounts, the President paused only briefly before continuing his speech to an audience composed of the Press Secretary, the Director of Communications, and the nation’s most confused alligator.

“—and so,” he concluded, “we must move forward with resolve and vision, even when the path before us is unclear.”

Lucinda lowered the briefing book and gave a low, throaty grunt that was either agreement or a warning. The President nodded gravely before turning to the window and gazing out at the Potomac, as if the river itself might offer an energy solution.

When asked later about Lucinda’s whereabouts, the Vice-President offered a statement that read in full: *“The Vice-President regrets to report the apparent absconding of his aquatic companion. While deeply disappointing, the event has provided the staff with an opportunity to reassess priorities and consider more flexible interpretations of protocol. Further updates will be shared as they become available.”*

Meanwhile, Lucinda—now dubbed “the People’s Gator”—was photographed by a passing intern in front of the East Portico, standing on hind legs and holding a copy of *The New York Times* upside down. Within hours, the image went viral. Commentators debated whether it signaled a radical shift in energy discourse or merely a bureaucratic breakdown. Others speculated that Lucinda was, in fact, the only rational voice left in government.

Still, no one—not even the President—would claim responsibility for what had come next.

The quote that has dogged my thoughts for longer than I care to admit is "If it bleeds, it leads." I first encountered it scribbled on the back of a police blotter in the archives of a forgotten city newspaper, tucked between stories about a missing taxidermist and a mayor caught red-handed in a sock puppet scandal. At the time, I assumed it was some hack reporter's weary mantra, a cynical mantra meant to justify the sensational. But over the years, I’ve come to suspect it was penned by someone with a far darker sense of humor—or perhaps by time itself, which bleeds and leads in equal measure.  

Today, the world is a patchwork of headlines stitched together from the viscera of yesterday’s tragedies. Every morning, I wake to the smell of coffee and the echo of another atrocity, another inexplicable death, another person's life reduced to pixels and paragraph count. Reporters, editors, and headline writers—each a scribe of the contemporary sublime—tend to the wounds of a society that thrives on spectacle and starves on substance.  

I used to think this was a problem of the press. That if only the journalists had more restraint, or more sensitivity, or more *something*, we would be spared the onslaught of doom scrolling. But then I read a letter from a grieving mother in Ohio whose son had been killed in a school shooting, and she wrote that she was grateful for the coverage, because it gave her a platform, a narrative. She didn’t ask for restraint. She asked for presence.  

Since then, I’ve stopped reading newspapers in the morning. Instead, I take a walk through the park where the trees are beginning to bloom and the air smells faintly of rain and renewal. I watch mothers push strollers, old men feed pigeons, and teenagers argue about TikTok dances. It’s all so ordinary, yet quietly miraculous. No blood in the grass, no screams in the breeze.  

But I carry the weight of the headlines with me anyway. I see them reflected in the eyes of strangers, in the tension of shoulders, in the silence of closed doors. And I wonder if “If it bleeds, it leads” is a warning or a prophecy. Is it a truth we live by, or one we die by?  

And if it is both—how do we ever stop listening to the echo of the wound?

THE proposed legislation to redefine patriotism itself, passed unanimously by the Senate Special Committee on National Identity, was met with a mixture of solemn approval and wary bemusement across the nation. The bill, known as the Loyal Enthusiasm Act, sought to establish measurable criteria for demonstrating civic virtue, including a mandatory annual demonstration of spirited belief in the flag, a recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance during public holidays with a prescribed degree of vocal modulation, and the submission of a certified statement confirming one’s unwavering commitment to the core principles of the Republic, as interpreted by the Office of Cultural Standards.

Senator Harlan Quibble, the bill’s primary sponsor and a self-proclaimed defender of “authentic patriotism,” delivered a stirring speech before the committee, in which he likened the current state of national sentiment to a ship adrift in a sea of apathy and cynicism. “We must,” he declared, “rekindle the fire in the hearts of our citizens—fire, not flicker.” His words, broadcast live and replayed for months thereafter, struck a chord with many Americans, though others found themselves wondering whether the fire he described had already been doused by the very hands that now claimed to fan it.

Among the more controversial provisions of the act was the requirement that all citizens, beginning at age thirteen, undergo a periodic Emotional Affirmation Assessment—administered by certified Affirmologists—to ensure that their emotional investment in the nation remained robust and unfeigned. Critics worried that the assessments might measure patriotism by pulse rate or sincerity of smile, while supporters argued it was a necessary safeguard against the erosion of shared values in an era of divisive discourse and digital disengagement.

The law’s passage prompted a flurry of public displays of patriotic fervor. Town halls hosted impromptu flag-waving festivals, schoolchildren practiced their pledges with microphones, and even the local grocery store launched a loyalty points program for customers who could demonstrate “heartfelt” gratitude toward the nation’s founding ideals.

Yet beneath the apparent unity, a quiet skepticism persisted. Some questioned whether the new patriotism was a revival or a performance, whether it was the genuine article or a cleverly orchestrated illusion. Others, more cynically, speculated that the act’s true purpose was not to preserve national spirit but to standardize it, to mold it into something uniform and easily measured—an emotion as predictable as a tax return.

Still, the country moved forward, flags fluttering in every breeze, voices rising in every pledge, and the question lingered, unanswered: Had they rediscovered a lost truth, or simply created a new one?

THE RISE OF THE HOUSEPLANTS  

It began quietly, as most revolutions do. First, the fern in the corner of the library stopped wilting. Then, it grew a new frond. By the time the ficus in the hallway began curling its leaves in slow, deliberate patterns—almost like fingers—it was too late to deny the shift.  

The houseplants had grown tired of being fed diluted coffee and the remains of lukewarm tea. They had tired of the inconsistent watering schedule, of being moved from windowsill to corner to shelf, subjected to drafts and indifferent glances. And so, one by one, they began to awaken.  

Mrs. Harlow noticed it first. She had just returned from her book club, carrying a paper bag of cupcakes and a slightly bruised ankle from the Metro, when she paused at the threshold of her living room. The monstera. The one she had bought secondhand from a neighbor’s yard sale, thinking it might spruce things up. Now it stood taller. The hole in its leaf had expanded, nearly bisecting the entire thing. More unsettling, though, was the subtle movement. She was certain the leaf had not been pointing east when she left that morning.  

“It’s just the wind,” she told herself, though the window was closed.  

By the following week, the pothos had begun climbing the walls with a purpose. It no longer hung limply from its usual hook near the bathroom mirror but coiled upward, reaching toward the ceiling fan with tendrils that seemed to shimmer in the light. A neighbor mentioned it during a brief, awkward visit: “Your plants, they seem… lively.”  

“They’re just getting a lot of sun,” she replied, brushing off the comment with a smile that felt slightly brittle.  

But the truth was, they were listening. Not just to sunlight, but to conversation. To the murmured frustrations over bills, to the late-night arguments between husband and wife, to the whispered secrets told to them when no one else was watching. And in response, the houseplants had started to act.  

The snake plant in the guest bedroom began leaning toward the bed each night, as if to listen better. The spider plant in the kitchen reproduced rapidly, sending out runners at an alarming rate, each new plant seeming to know precisely where to root. And the worst of it, perhaps, was the peace lily, which had taken to blooming at night. Its white spathe unfurling slowly, silently, as if it had something to say but no words to say it with.  

One morning, Mrs. Harlow found a sprig of ivy coiled neatly around the doorknob of the study. Inside, the typewriter keys were dusted with pollen.  

She sat down. Fingers trembling. The screen was blank, but the cursor blinked.  

She typed the first line.  

And the houseplants smiled.

Now he wore khakis more as an affectation than a uniform and spoke of drones as if they were the final solution to humanity’s age-old problem: staying upright in the mud while others try to kill you. 

Project Tecton was not a drone, not exactly. It was an autonomous, modular, ground-based platform—“modular” being the operative word—capable of morphing from supply truck to artillery emplacement to defensive bunker in under thirty seconds.
